title: Morphological Variability of Helicoverpa armigera (Hubner) on different Host Plants
authors: Archana Singh, Dr. Moti Chandra Yadav
affiliations: Government Girls Degree College Shahganj, Jaunpur (U.P.)

blocks.x: ABSTRACT:

Hosted a field trail during kharif/rabi-2022-23 to investigate the morphological variability of Helicoverpa armigera (Hubner) on several hosts. Across various host plants, the mean larval weight of H. armigera varied between 241.1 and 323.3 mg. The two hosts with the highest larval weights, chickpea and cotton, were 323.3 and 303.9 mg, respectively.

Across various host plants, the mean larval length of H. armigera varied between 23.4 and 29.85 mm. The greatest larval lengths of the larvae obtained from cotton, red gramme, and chickpea were 29.85, 29.70, and 29.20 mm, respectively. Across various host plants, the mean larval width of H. armigera varied between 1.70 and 2.59 mm. The larvae obtained from pigeonpea, cotton, and okra had the greatest larval widths among the various hosts, measuring 2.59, 2.40, and 2.37 mm, respectively.
A higher percentage of greenish-colored larvae (23.5%) was seen regardless of the host plants. Dark green (32.0%), bright green (12.0%), and greenish brown (12.0%) colours came next.
Key words: Morphological, Colour Morphs, Helicoverpa armigera.
OVERVIEW:

The worldwide, polyphagous, and infamous Helicoverpa armigera (Hubner) pest is found across the tropics and sub-tropics and affects a wide variety of crops of agricultural significance. The behaviour of H. armigera populations infesting different host plants and geographically separate groups varies to such an extent that it is impossible to rule out the possibility of at least subspecific differences across populations (Reed and Pawar, 1982). Within and across populations of H. armigera obtained from various hosts, there have been continuous differences in the morphological criteria that warranted particular isolation (Bhatnagar and Davies, 1978; Bhattacharjee and Gupta, 1972). The morphological diversity of H. armigera on various host plants was investigated.
SUPPLIES AND TECHNIQUES:

To examine the morphological differences, twenty H. armigera larvae were chosen at random from ten distinct hosts—sunflower, maize, sorghum, chilli, tomato, chickpea, safflower, pigeonpea, cotton, and okra—at the pre-pupal stage. Using a scale, the larvae's length and width were measured in millimetres. Using a microbalance, the larvae's weight was measured in milligrammes. By comparing to a colour chart, the larval colour of every noticeable colour form seen in H. armigera populations was taken into consideration and visual servations were taken into account.

Chickpeas had the largest larval range (232-424 mg), while safflower had the smallest (228-289 mg) (Table 1). Among the several host plants, the average larval length of H. armigera varied between 23.4 and 29.85 mm. The greatest larval lengths of the larvae obtained from cotton, chickpeas, and pigeonpeas were 29.20 mm, 29.85 mm, and 29.70 mm, respectively. The larvae obtained from tomatoes (25.75 mm), sunflowers (27.3 mm), and okra (28.4 mm) came next. The larvae gathered from sorghum had the smallest documented larval length (23.4 mm). Overall, the larvae taken from maize (15–38 mm) showed the broadest range, whereas the larvae collected from chickpeas (24–36 mm) and cotton (23–35 mm) showed the shortest range (Table 2). Across various host plants, the mean larval width of H. armigera varied between 1.70 and 2.59 mm. The larvae obtained from okra, cotton, and pigeonpea had the greatest larval widths among the various hosts, measuring 2.59, 2.40, and 2.37, respectively. mm, in that order. The tomato (2.17 mm) and chilli (2.33 mm) came next. The larvae gathered from maize had the smallest known larval width (1.70 mm). Overall, the larvae taken from okra (1.9-3.1 mm) showed the narrowest range, whereas the larvae collected from pigeonpea (1-3.1 mm) showed the broadest range (Table 3). The current results are consistent with the findings of Uthamasamy et al. (1988), who stated that the length of fully grown larvae was approximately 35–42 mm. According to Suvarna Patil (2005), cotton (299.2 mg), pigeonpea (300.2 mg), and chickpea (305.8 mg) had the highest larval weights. Cotton (30.98 mm), pigeonpea (31.33 mm), and chickpea (31.44 mm) all had noticeably greater larval lengths. According to Vijaykumar (2005), the weight and length of the larvae in H. Armigera differed greatly amongst the geographical areas. Additionally, the two-year pooled data showed that Madurai had the lowest larval weight (480.07 44.14 mg), whereas Guntur had the significantly heaviest (505.75 + 58.51 mg), comparable to Raichur (501.40 + 49.13 mg). On cotton, the Raichur location also had the considerably greatest larval length (27.08 ± 2.95 mm), followed by Guntur, while Madurai had the lowest length (22.12 ± 2.22 mm).

Table 4 lists the various body colour variants found in the field population along with their relative frequencies. According to the findings, certain colour morphs are more prevalent in various hosts. A larger percentage (23.5%) of greenish-colored larvae was seen regardless of the host plants. Dark green (32.0%), bright green (12.0%), and greenish brown (12.0%) came next. White (1.5%) and reddish brown (3.5%) varieties gathered from sorghum, safflower, and maize showed the lowest colour.

All hosts exhibited morphs of light green, dark green, and greenish hues. While yellowish colour variants were observed in sunflower (20%), maize (15%), safflower (10%), pigeonpea (10%), chilli (5%), and cotton (5%), whitish colour morphs were found in maize (5%), cotton (5%), and chilli (5%) as well as sunflower. Larvae of the blackish brown colour morph were found in 15% sunflower and 5% chilli. Maize (10%), chickpeas (10%), okra (10%), cotton (10%), sunflower (5%), tomato (5%), and sorghum (5%), all had brownish-colored larvae. Chickpeas (25), pigeonpeas (20%), okra (20%), chilli (15%), sorghum (10%), tomato (10%), safflower (10%), and cotton (10%) were found to harbour greenish brown larvae. Cotton and maize had the most colour morphs (8) among the various hosts, followed by sunflower (7), chilli (7), and safflower (7). The remaining host plants had six colour morphs.

Nagaraja Rao and Abraham (1956), who noted that the larval hue varied greatly from velvety black to yellowish green, lend credence to the current study. A fully grown caterpillar has dark brown lines running the length of its body and is greenish in colour (Gopalan and Venugopal, 1972). According to Uthamasamy et al. (1988), Broadley (1977) noted a significant range of colouration in the larvae, from extremely dark to light green or pink, and from green, f fawn, pink, yellow, or brown. Larval colouration was tightly linked to nutrition; when raised on cotton, corn, tomato and tobacco, the larvae displayed unique colours and markings. B-carotene was added to the artificial diet, which either induced different larval colour forms to develop sooner or increased the dorsal and stigmatal colouration (Ramos & Morallo-Rajesus, 1976). When they were fed, green morphs quickly turned yellow, according to Maragal (1990), but black morphs kept part of their pigment.
However, the colour character was found to be genetically controlled by Bartlett and Raulston (1982) from the United States.

Ten distinct body colour morphs were seen in various host plants, according to Suvarna Patil (2005). Greenish (24.8%) and dark green (16.5%) colour morphs were found to be more prevalent than other colour morphs, with an average number of 6.1. The field populations of cotton bollworms, H. armigera, were found to have nine distinct body colour morphs over the course of two years in various locations. Regardless of the location, greenish (30.99 and 28.15% respectively) and blackish green (23.42 and 25.61% respectively) morphs were significantly more prevalent than other colours, followed by greenish brown (18.47 and 19.21% respectively). The current results are consistent with the reports mentioned above.

According to previous research, H. armigera's general larval colour is thought to be a changeable feature that varies depending on the type of food it consumes. Nonetheless, it was inevitable that the unique colour patterns and pigmentation were controlled by genetics. Other colour patterns were discovered to vary in the background of the same food in the current findings, aside from the basic body colour. This could be because the food was consumed in different plant sections, such as squares, flowers, bolls, heads, pods, capsules, fruits, and infrequently, leaves. Regarding the intermediate larval colour morphs, the colour shift was fairly erratic and most likely greatly impacted by the components of the host plant.

Nagaraja Rao and Abraham (1956), Gopalan and Venugopal (1972), Lewin et al. (1973), Singh and Singh (1975), and Thulsi Jyoti (1991) have also documented hue changes, both within the stadium and between instars. In the current investigation, however, comparable variation was discovered with intermediate forms. Even Ramos and Morallo-Rajesus (1976) found that B-carotene enhanced the stigmata and dorsal colouring, which seems to apply to intermediate forms instead of pure inbreeds. Broadly (1977) noted that the larvae had a wide range of colours, from extremely dark to light green or pink, and from green, fawn, pink, yellow, or brown. Despite being polyphagous, H. armigera's selection for a specific host was found to be highly dependent on the temporal and spatial availability of host plants during the feeding stage of development, according to Pearson (1958) and Roome (1975).
